purpose: Romosozumab-aqqg is used to treat osteoporosis in women who have gone through menopause and are at high risk of breaking a bone. It helps make bones stronger and reduces the chance of fractures, especially in the spine and hip. Doctors often prescribe it when other osteoporosis treatments have not worked well enough.
how_it_works: Your body has a protein called sclerostin that slows down bone building. This medication blocks that protein, which allows your body to build new bone more quickly while also slowing down bone loss at the same time. Think of it like releasing the brakes on your bone-building system so your bones can get stronger faster.
common_side_effects: Joint pain, muscle pain, headache, and reactions at the injection site such as redness, swelling, or discomfort are the most commonly reported side effects. Some people may also experience fatigue or back pain.
warnings: This medication carries an important warning about a possible increased risk of heart attack and stroke, so it is generally not recommended if you have had a heart attack or stroke in the past year. It can also rarely cause a serious jaw bone problem called osteonecrosis of the jaw, and an unusual thigh bone fracture. Tell your doctor about all your medications and any dental procedures planned. Treatment is limited to 12 monthly doses due to these risks.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is two injections given one right after the other by your healthcare provider once a month, for a total of 12 months. Each injection is given just under the skin, typically in the stomach, thigh, or upper arm. After completing the 12-month course, your doctor will likely switch you to a different bone-strengthening medication to maintain your results.
